anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.front: Which three bones fuse to form each hip bone, and where do they meet?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.back: The ilium, ischium & pubis, fused at the acetabulum (via the triradiate cartilage until puberty).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.front: How do the bones of the pelvic ring articulate?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.back: The hip bones join the sacrum at the sacroiliac joints posteriorly and each other at the pubic symphysis anteriorly.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.front: Distinguish the greater (false) from the lesser (true) pelvis.
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.back: The greater pelvis lies above the pelvic inlet (part of the abdominal cavity); the lesser pelvis lies below it and contains the pelvic viscera and birth canal.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.front: What are the borders of the pelvic inlet (brim)?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.back: Posterior = sacral promontory & ala; lateral = linea terminalis (arcuate line + pectineal line); anterior = pubic symphysis & crest.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.front: What is the linea terminalis composed of?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.back: The arcuate line of the ilium plus the pectineal line (pecten pubis) of the superior pubic ramus — the lateral border of the pelvic inlet.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.front: What are the borders of the pelvic outlet?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.back: Posterior = tip of the coccyx; lateral = ischial tuberosities; posterolateral = sacrotuberous ligaments; anterior = pubic arch.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.front: What is the obstetric conjugate, and why can't it be measured directly?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.back: The distance from the sacral promontory to the most posterosuperior point of the pubic symphysis — the narrowest fixed AP inlet diameter (~10.5 cm); it lies behind the symphysis so is estimated from the diagonal conjugate (~1.5–2 cm longer, measured per vaginam). The true (anatomical) conjugate runs to the superior symphyseal margin and is slightly longer.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.front: Which is usually the narrowest part of the whole birth canal?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.back: The interspinous distance — between the two ischial spines.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.front: Give three features distinguishing the female from the male pelvis.
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.back: The female pelvis has a wider subpubic angle (>80°, U-shaped), a rounder/oval inlet, a wider greater sciatic notch (~90°), everted ischial spines and a shallower cavity.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.front: Name the four Caldwell–Moloy pelvic shapes.
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.back: Gynaecoid (round, ideal for delivery), android (heart-shaped/male), anthropoid (oval, long AP) and platypelloid (flat, wide transverse).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.front: Where does the sacrospinous ligament attach?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.back: From the sacrum & coccyx to the ischial spine.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.front: Where does the sacrotuberous ligament attach?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.back: From the sacrum & coccyx to the ischial tuberosity.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.front: What do the sacrospinous and sacrotuberous ligaments create?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.back: They convert the greater & lesser sciatic notches into the greater & lesser sciatic foramina (and resist backward rotation of the sacrum).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.front: What is the functional difference between the greater and lesser sciatic foramina?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.back: The greater is the main exit from the pelvis to the gluteal region; the lesser is the route into the perineum (the pudendal nerve & internal pudendal vessels hook around the ischial spine to re-enter here).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.front: What is the key landmark within the greater sciatic foramen?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.back: Piriformis — structures pass above or below it.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.front: What exits ABOVE piriformis in the greater sciatic foramen?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.back: The superior gluteal nerve & vessels.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.front: List the structures exiting BELOW piriformis.
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.back: Inferior gluteal nerve & vessels, the sciatic nerve, posterior femoral cutaneous nerve, nerve to quadratus femoris, pudendal nerve & internal pudendal vessels, and the nerve to obturator internus.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.front: What passes through the lesser sciatic foramen?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.back: The tendon of obturator internus, the nerve to obturator internus, and the pudendal nerve & internal pudendal vessels re-entering the perineum.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.front: Which muscle forms the lateral wall of the pelvis, and what canal lies there?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.back: Obturator internus (with obturator fascia & membrane); the obturator canal transmits the obturator nerve & vessels to the thigh.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.front: Which muscle forms the posterior pelvic wall, and what lies on it?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.back: Piriformis — the sacral plexus lies on its anterior surface.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.front: What muscles make up the pelvic floor (pelvic diaphragm)?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.back: Levator ani (puborectalis, pubococcygeus & iliococcygeus) plus coccygeus (ischiococcygeus).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.front: From where does levator ani arise?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.back: From the tendinous arch (a thickening of obturator fascia) running from the pubis to the ischial spine.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.front: What is the nerve supply of levator ani?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.back: The nerve to levator ani (S3–S4) and branches of the pudendal nerve.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.front: What are the two hiatuses in the pelvic floor?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.back: The urogenital hiatus (urethra ± vagina) and the anal hiatus (anal canal).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.front: How does puborectalis contribute to continence?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.back: It forms a sling around the anorectal junction maintaining the anorectal angle (~80–90°); relaxation opens the angle to allow defecation.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.front: What is the perineal body?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.back: The central tendon of the perineum — a fibromuscular node anterior to the anal canal where the pelvic floor and perineal muscles converge; the key structure torn in a perineal tear / cut in an episiotomy.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.front: Classify the sacroiliac joint.
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.back: A compound joint: part synovial (anteriorly) and part syndesmosis (the strong posterior interosseous ligament); very stable with little movement.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.front: Classify the pubic symphysis and describe its behaviour in pregnancy.
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.back: A secondary cartilaginous joint (fibrocartilage disc); relaxin loosens it (and the SI joints) in pregnancy to widen the outlet (can cause symphysis pubis dysfunction).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.front: Why is the pelvic floor clinically important in women?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.back: Damage (childbirth, pudendal injury) causes pelvic organ prolapse and stress urinary incontinence.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.front: The ovarian/testicular (gonadal) arteries arise from the aorta at which level?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.back: At ~L2, just inferior to the renal arteries — they then descend on the posterior abdominal wall to the gonads.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.front: What is the trigone of the bladder?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.back: A smooth triangular area of the bladder base bounded by the two ureteric orifices and the internal urethral orifice; it is sensitive to stretch.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.front: What is the median umbilical ligament?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.back: The fibrous remnant of the urachus, running from the apex of the bladder to the umbilicus.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.front: What muscle forms the bladder wall, and what is the retropubic space?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.back: The detrusor (smooth muscle); the retropubic space (of Retzius) is the extraperitoneal fat-filled space between the bladder and the pubic symphysis.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.front: Describe the two urethral sphincters.
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.back: The internal urethral sphincter (smooth muscle at the bladder neck; involuntary, prevents retrograde ejaculation in the male) and the external urethral sphincter (skeletal muscle in the deep perineal pouch; voluntary, pudendal nerve).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.front: What is the effect of PARASYMPATHETIC stimulation on the bladder?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.back: Detrusor contracts and the internal sphincter relaxes → voiding (“S2,3,4 empties the bladder”).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.front: What is the effect of SYMPATHETIC stimulation on the bladder?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.back: Detrusor relaxes and the internal sphincter contracts → storage/continence (and prevents retrograde ejaculation).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.front: Where does the ureter cross into the pelvis?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.back: At the bifurcation of the common iliac artery, over the pelvic brim; it then runs down the lateral pelvic wall.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.front: Name the three sites of ureteric constriction.
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.back: The pelviureteric junction (PUJ), where it crosses the pelvic brim/iliac vessels, and the vesicoureteric junction (VUJ) — the narrowest.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.front: Describe the relationship of the ureter to the uterine artery, and its significance.
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.back: The uterine artery crosses anterior (superior) to the ureter near the cervix (“water under the bridge”) — the ureter is at risk of ligation during hysterectomy.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.front: Why does the ureter pierce the bladder wall obliquely?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.back: The oblique passage acts as a physiological (flap) valve that is compressed as the bladder fills, preventing vesicoureteric reflux.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.front: Name the four parts of the male urethra in order.
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.back: Pre-prostatic → prostatic → membranous → spongy (penile).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.front: Which part of the male urethra is the widest, and which the least distensible?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.back: The prostatic part is widest (receives the ejaculatory ducts); the membranous part is shortest and least distensible (through the external sphincter) — the commonest site of iatrogenic injury.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.front: Why is the female more prone to ascending UTIs?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.back: The female urethra is short (~4 cm) and straight, allowing easier ascent of bacteria to the bladder.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.front: At what level does the rectum begin, and what is its dilated distal part called?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.back: At S3 (continuous with the sigmoid colon); the dilated distal portion is the ampulla.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.front: Describe the peritoneal covering of the rectum.
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.back: Peritoneum covers the upper third anteriorly & laterally, the middle third anteriorly only, and the lower third is subperitoneal (no peritoneum).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.front: Give the arterial supply of the rectum.
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.back: Superior rectal (from the inferior mesenteric artery), middle rectal (from the internal iliac) and inferior rectal (from the internal pudendal) arteries.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.front: What is the clinical significance of the pectinate (dentate) line?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.back: It divides the anal canal: above = visceral (autonomic) innervation, insensate, portal venous drainage, columnar epithelium (internal, painless haemorrhoids); below = somatic (inferior rectal) innervation, very sensitive, systemic drainage, squamous epithelium (external, painful haemorrhoids/fissures).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.front: Name the three parts of the uterus.
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.back: The fundus, body (containing the cavity) and cervix.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.front: Name the three layers of the uterine wall.
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.back: Endometrium (mucosa, shed in menstruation), myometrium (smooth muscle) and perimetrium (peritoneal serosa).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.front: What is the normal position of the uterus?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.back: Anteverted (the cervix tips forward relative to the vagina) and anteflexed (the body is flexed forward on the cervix).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.front: Name the parts of the uterine (Fallopian) tube from lateral to medial.
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.back: Infundibulum (with fimbriae) → ampulla → isthmus → intramural (uterine) part.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.front: Where does fertilisation usually occur, and where is the commonest site of ectopic pregnancy?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.back: Both in the ampulla of the uterine tube.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.front: What does the suspensory ligament of the ovary carry?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.back: The ovarian vessels (and nerves/lymphatics) — it runs from the ovary to the pelvic side wall over the brim; the ovarian ligament tethers the ovary to the uterus.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.front: Describe the blood supply of the uterus and vagina.
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.back: The uterine artery (from the internal iliac) supplies the uterus and gives a vaginal branch; the vagina is also supplied by the vaginal artery (usually a direct branch of the internal iliac). The uterine artery anastomoses with the ovarian artery (from the aorta).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.front: What is the round ligament of the uterus, and its course?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.back: A remnant of the gubernaculum running from the uterine horn, through the deep inguinal ring & inguinal canal, to the labium majus (helps maintain anteversion).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.front: What is the broad ligament?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.back: A double fold of peritoneum draping over the uterus, tubes & ovaries — subdivided into the mesometrium, mesosalpinx & mesovarium.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.front: What are the true structural supports of the cervix/uterus?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.back: The transverse cervical (cardinal) and uterosacral ligaments (condensations of endopelvic fascia).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.front: What is the rectouterine pouch, and why is it important?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.back: The pouch of Douglas (between uterus & rectum) — the lowest point of the peritoneal cavity in the female; fluid/blood/pus collects here and can be sampled via the posterior vaginal fornix (culdocentesis).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.front: Which zone of the prostate gives rise to most cancers, and which to BPH?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.back: The peripheral zone (posterior) → most carcinomas (palpable on PR); the transitional (periurethral) zone → benign prostatic hyperplasia.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.front: How is the ejaculatory duct formed, and where does it open?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.back: By the union of the ductus (vas) deferens and the duct of the seminal vesicle; it opens into the prostatic urethra (at the seminal colliculus).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.front: From which spinal roots is the sacral plexus formed?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.back: The anterior rami of L4–S4, with the lumbosacral trunk (L4–L5) linking it to the lumbar plexus.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.front: Where does the sacral plexus lie?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.back: On the piriformis muscle on the posterior pelvic wall, anterior to the sacrum; most branches leave via the greater sciatic foramen.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.front: What are the roots of the sciatic nerve, and what does it supply?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.back: L4–S3 (the largest nerve in the body); it supplies the hamstrings and — via its tibial & common fibular divisions — all of the leg and foot.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.front: What are the roots of the superior and inferior gluteal nerves, and what do they supply?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.back: Superior gluteal (L4–S1) → gluteus medius, minimus & TFL; inferior gluteal (L5–S2) → gluteus maximus.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.front: What are the roots of the pudendal nerve?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.back: S2, S3 & S4 (“S2,3,4 keeps the pelvis off the floor”).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.front: Describe the course of the pudendal nerve.
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.back: It exits the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen (below piriformis), hooks around the ischial spine / sacrospinous ligament, re-enters via the lesser sciatic foramen, and runs in the pudendal (Alcock’s) canal on the lateral wall of the ischioanal fossa.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.front: Name the three main branches of the pudendal nerve.
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.back: The inferior rectal nerve, the perineal nerve, and the dorsal nerve of the penis/clitoris.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.front: What is the overall function of the pudendal nerve?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.back: The main somatic nerve of the perineum: motor to the perineal & pelvic-floor muscles and both external sphincters, and sensory to the perineum & external genitalia — essential for continence & sexual sensation.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.front: Where is a pudendal nerve block performed, and why?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.back: At the ischial spine (palpated transvaginally), where the nerve hooks around it — to provide perineal analgesia for the second stage of labour, instrumental delivery or perineal repair.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.front: What forms the coccygeal plexus, and what does it supply?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.back: S4, S5 & the coccygeal nerve; it gives the anococcygeal nerves (skin over the coccyx) and twigs to coccygeus & part of levator ani.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.front: What are the pelvic splanchnic nerves, and what is special about them?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.back: The parasympathetic outflow of the pelvis (nervi erigentes, S2–S4) — the only parasympathetic fibres arising from the sacral spinal cord rather than a cranial nerve.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.front: What are the functions of the parasympathetic (pelvic splanchnic) supply?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.back: Detrusor contraction (voiding), erection, and hindgut & rectal motility (contracts the rectal wall, relaxes the internal anal sphincter).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.front: How do parasympathetic fibres reach the hindgut?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.back: Some pelvic splanchnic fibres ascend through the inferior & superior hypogastric plexuses to the inferior mesenteric plexus, supplying the descending/sigmoid colon & rectum.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.front: What is the sympathetic supply to the pelvis, and its origin?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.back: From the T10/T12–L2 segments via the superior hypogastric plexus (a continuation of the aortic plexus) and the sacral splanchnic nerves (from the sacral sympathetic trunk, ending at the ganglion impar).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.front: What are the functions of the sympathetic supply to the pelvis?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.back: Ejaculation (emission), vasoconstriction, and internal urethral sphincter contraction (urine storage / continence).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.front: Where is the superior hypogastric plexus, and what does it become?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.back: A midline plexus anterior to the sacral promontory / lower aorta; it divides into the right & left hypogastric nerves (mainly sympathetic).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.front: What forms the inferior hypogastric plexus, and where does it lie?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.back: The hypogastric nerve (sympathetic) + pelvic splanchnic nerves (parasympathetic) + sacral splanchnics; it lies as a paired plexus on either side of the rectum (near the cervix/prostate).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.front: What sub-plexuses arise from the inferior hypogastric plexus?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.back: Organ-specific plexuses: rectal, vesical, prostatic and uterovaginal (Frankenhäuser).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.front: Summarise the autonomic control of the bladder.
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.back: Parasympathetic (S2–4) → detrusor contracts → voiding; sympathetic (L1–2) → detrusor relaxes & internal sphincter contracts → storage.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.front: Explain the “point and shoot” mnemonic.
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.back: Parasympathetic = Point (erection); Sympathetic = Shoot (emission/ejaculation).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.front: Which autonomic division controls erection, and what is the clinical consequence of damage?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.back: The parasympathetic (pelvic splanchnic/cavernous nerves); damage (e.g. during prostatectomy) → erectile dysfunction — hence nerve-sparing surgery.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.front: What causes retrograde ejaculation?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.back: Damage to the sympathetic supply (e.g. after retroperitoneal surgery) → the internal urethral sphincter fails to close, so semen passes backwards into the bladder.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.front: What determines whether pelvic visceral pain travels sympathetically or parasympathetically?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.back: The pelvic pain line (the inferior limit of the peritoneum): structures touching peritoneum (above) → sympathetic afferents; subperitoneal structures (below) → parasympathetic afferents.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.front: Where is pain from ABOVE the pelvic pain line referred?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.back: Via sympathetic afferents to T12–L2 → the suprapubic region & lower back (e.g. the uterine body, upper bladder).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.front: Where is pain from BELOW the pelvic pain line referred?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.back: Via parasympathetic (pelvic splanchnic) afferents to S2–S4 → the perineum (e.g. the cervix, bladder trigone, lower rectum).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.front: How is pain transmitted in the two stages of labour?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.back: First stage (uterine body/cervix) via T10–L1 (& S2–4) — hence a lumbar epidural; second stage (perineal distension) via the pudendal nerve (S2–4) — hence a pudendal block.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.front: What is cauda equina syndrome and why is it an emergency?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.back: Compression of the cauda equina (lumbosacral nerve roots), characteristically involving the S2–S4 roots → saddle anaesthesia, painless urinary retention and bowel/sexual dysfunction (± lower-limb weakness); a surgical emergency requiring urgent decompression.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.front: What is pudendal neuralgia?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.back: Chronic burning perineal pain from pudendal nerve compression (e.g. in Alcock’s canal — “cyclist’s syndrome”).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.front: Which nerves supply the pelvic floor (levator ani)?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.back: The nerve to levator ani (S3–S4) and branches of the pudendal nerve.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.front: What is the ganglion impar?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.back: The single midline ganglion where the two sacral sympathetic trunks converge, anterior to the coccyx (a target for blocks in perineal/coccygeal pain).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.front: What is the main arterial supply of the pelvis, and where does it arise?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.back: The internal iliac artery, arising where the common iliac artery bifurcates at the pelvic brim (~L5/S1).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.front: Into what two divisions does the internal iliac artery split?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.back: An anterior division (mostly visceral branches) and a posterior division (parietal branches).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.front: Name the three branches of the POSTERIOR division of the internal iliac artery.
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.back: Iliolumbar, lateral sacral & superior gluteal arteries (“I Love Sex”).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.front: List the main branches of the ANTERIOR division of the internal iliac artery.
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.back: Umbilical (→ superior vesical), obturator, inferior vesical (♂) / vaginal (♀), middle rectal, uterine (♀), internal pudendal and inferior gluteal.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.front: Which four internal-iliac branches leave the pelvis, and by what routes?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.back: The superior gluteal, inferior gluteal & internal pudendal (via the greater sciatic foramen) and the obturator artery (via the obturator canal).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.front: Which internal-iliac branch exits ABOVE piriformis?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.back: The superior gluteal artery; the inferior gluteal and internal pudendal exit below piriformis.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.front: What is the corona mortis?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.back: An aberrant/accessory obturator artery (~20%) arising from the inferior epigastric artery, crossing the superior pubic ramus — at risk of injury in femoral hernia repair or pelvic fracture (“crown of death”).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.front: Where do the gonadal (ovarian/testicular) arteries arise?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.back: From the abdominal aorta at ~L2 (following the gonads' embryological origin).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.front: What is the superior rectal artery a continuation of?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.back: The inferior mesenteric artery — it supplies the rectum down to the pectinate line (upper & middle rectum).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.front: What are the branches and territory of the internal pudendal artery?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.back: The chief artery of the perineum (runs with the pudendal nerve in Alcock’s canal); branches: inferior rectal, perineal, and the dorsal & deep arteries of the penis/clitoris (deep arteries fill the erectile tissue).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.front: Describe the rectal arterial anastomosis and its clinical relevance.
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.back: The superior rectal (from the IMA), middle rectal and inferior rectal (from the internal iliac/internal pudendal) arteries anastomose around the anorectum, giving the rectum a rich collateral supply. (The corresponding venous anastomosis is the portosystemic site of rectal varices.)

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.front: Why can the internal iliac artery be safely ligated?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.back: A rich collateral anastomosis (rectal, uterine–ovarian and cruciate/trochanteric) keeps the pelvis perfused — used for intractable pelvic or postpartum haemorrhage.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.front: How do the pelvic viscera drain venously?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.back: Via interconnected valveless venous plexuses (rectal, vesical, prostatic, uterine, vaginal) into the internal iliac veins → common iliac → IVC.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.front: Where does the superior rectal vein drain, and why does it matter?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.back: Into the portal system (inferior mesenteric vein) — a portosystemic anastomosis with the systemic middle/inferior rectal veins (rectal varices).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.front: Where do the right and left gonadal veins drain?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.back: The right gonadal vein → IVC; the left gonadal vein → left renal vein.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.front: What is Batson's plexus, and its clinical importance?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.back: The valveless internal vertebral venous plexus, which communicates with the pelvic plexuses — a route for prostate/pelvic cancer to metastasise to the vertebrae, pelvis & brain (bypassing the IVC and lungs).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.front: What is the main lymphatic pathway of the pelvic viscera?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.back: Most drain to the internal iliac nodes → common iliac → lateral aortic/lumbar (para-aortic) nodes → lumbar trunks → cisterna chyli/thoracic duct.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.front: Where do the ovaries, testes and uterine tubes drain lymph, and why?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.back: Directly to the para-aortic (lumbar) nodes, following the gonadal vessels back to their embryological origin — not the inguinal nodes.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.front: Why is the gonadal lymphatic drainage clinically crucial?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.back: Testicular (and ovarian) cancer spreads first to the para-aortic nodes; scrotal/vulval skin cancer, by contrast, drains to the superficial inguinal nodes.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.front: Which structures drain to the superficial inguinal nodes?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.back: The superficial perineum, lower vagina, lower anal canal (below the pectinate line), scrotum & vulva, and the lower limb.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.front: How does the pectinate line divide anal canal lymphatic drainage?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.back: Above the pectinate line → internal iliac nodes; below → superficial inguinal nodes.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.front: Describe the lymphatic drainage of the different parts of the uterus.
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.back: Fundus & tubal angle → para-aortic nodes (+ along the round ligament to superficial inguinal); body → external iliac; cervix → internal/external iliac + sacral nodes.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.front: What do the external iliac nodes mainly receive?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.back: Lymph from the lower limb (via the inguinal nodes) and deeper anterior abdominal/pelvic structures; they drain into the common iliac nodes.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.front: What is the significance of the uterine artery crossing the ureter?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.back: The uterine artery (from the internal iliac) crosses over the ureter near the cervix — the ureter is at risk of ligation during hysterectomy (“water under the bridge”).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.front: Which artery supplies the erectile tissue, and via which branch?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.back: The internal pudendal artery, via the deep arteries of the penis/clitoris (to the corpora cavernosa).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.front: What causes ovarian vein thrombosis, and how does it present?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.back: A postpartum complication (usually right-sided) presenting with flank/lower abdominal pain and fever.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.front: Which nodes drain the posterior pelvic wall and part of the rectum?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.back: The sacral nodes (along the median & lateral sacral vessels).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.front: Which vessels does the obturator artery accompany, and through which opening?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.back: The obturator nerve, through the obturator canal, to the medial thigh.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.front: What is the medial umbilical ligament derived from?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.back: The obliterated distal part of the umbilical artery (a branch of the anterior division of the internal iliac).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.front: Summarise where prostate cancer and testicular cancer characteristically metastasise.
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.back: Prostate cancer → the bony spine/pelvis (via Batson’s valveless veins; sclerotic mets); testicular cancer → the para-aortic nodes (via gonadal lymphatics).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.front: What are the boundaries of the perineum?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.back: A diamond bounded by the pubic symphysis (anterior), the ischial tuberosities (lateral) and the coccyx (posterior).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.front: How is the perineum divided into two triangles?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.back: A line between the ischial tuberosities divides it into the anterior urogenital (UG) triangle and the posterior anal triangle.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.front: What does the urogenital triangle contain?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.back: The external genitalia, urethra (& vagina), the perineal membrane and the superficial & deep perineal pouches.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.front: What does the anal triangle contain?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.back: The anal canal, external anal sphincter and the paired ischioanal fossae.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.front: What is the perineal membrane?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.back: A tough triangular fascial sheet spanning the UG triangle, attached to the pubic arch; it is perforated by the urethra (& vagina) and anchors the erectile bodies.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.front: What is the perineal body and why is it important?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.back: A fibromuscular central tendon at the junction of the two triangles (anterior to the anus) — the anchoring point for the perineal muscles, external anal sphincter & levator ani; torn in childbirth and incised in a midline episiotomy (the mediolateral episiotomy deliberately spares it).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.front: What are the boundaries and contents of the superficial perineal pouch?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.back: Between the perineal membrane and Colles’ fascia; it contains the erectile tissues (crura & bulb), the superficial perineal muscles, the greater vestibular (Bartholin’s) glands (♀), and branches of the internal pudendal vessels & pudendal nerve.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.front: What are the boundaries and contents of the deep perineal pouch?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.back: Between the perineal membrane and the pelvic floor; it contains the external urethral sphincter, the deep transverse perinei, the membranous urethra and the bulbourethral (Cowper’s) glands (♂).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.front: Name the superficial perineal muscles.
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.back: Superficial transverse perinei, bulbospongiosus & ischiocavernosus.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.front: What is the action of bulbospongiosus?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.back: In the male it empties the urethra & aids erection; in the female it constricts the vaginal orifice (it covers the bulb/corpus spongiosum).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.front: What is the action of ischiocavernosus?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.back: It compresses the crura (corpora cavernosa) to maintain erection by impeding venous outflow.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.front: What is the nerve supply of all the perineal muscles?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.back: The pudendal nerve (S2–S4) — via its perineal & inferior rectal branches.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.front: Which muscles occupy the deep perineal pouch?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.back: The external urethral sphincter (voluntary micturition control) and the deep transverse perinei (supports the perineal body).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.front: Name the erectile bodies of the penis.
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.back: Two corpora cavernosa (dorsal, with crura anchored to the ischiopubic rami) and one corpus spongiosum (ventral, containing the spongy urethra, with the bulb proximally & the glans distally).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.front: Which muscles cover the crura and the bulb respectively?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.back: Ischiocavernosus covers the crura (corpora cavernosa); bulbospongiosus covers the bulb (corpus spongiosum).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.front: Give the female homologues of the male erectile structures and glands.
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.back: The clitoris (corpora cavernosa/crura), the bulbs of the vestibule (penile bulb/corpus spongiosum) and the greater vestibular (Bartholin’s) glands (bulbourethral glands).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.front: What is the ischioanal fossa?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.back: A paired, wedge-shaped, fat-filled space either side of the anal canal, bounded by levator ani & obturator internus, that lets the anal canal distend during defecation; the two fossae communicate posteriorly.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.front: What are the contents of the ischioanal fossa?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.back: The inferior rectal vessels & nerves, and the pudendal (Alcock’s) canal in the lateral wall (carrying the pudendal nerve & internal pudendal vessels).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.front: Why is the ischioanal fossa clinically important?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.back: Its fat is a common site of infection (ischioanal abscess); because the fossae communicate posteriorly, infection can form a horseshoe abscess or a fistula-in-ano.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.front: Compare the internal and external anal sphincters.
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.back: The internal anal sphincter = smooth muscle, involuntary (tonic at rest, relaxed by parasympathetics); the external anal sphincter = skeletal muscle, voluntary (pudendal/inferior rectal nerve), blending with puborectalis.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.front: What is Colles' fascia, and its clinical relevance?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.back: The superficial perineal fascia (membranous layer) forming the floor of the superficial pouch; continuous with Scarpa’s fascia — a ruptured bulbar urethra spills urine into the pouch, tracking to the scrotum & abdominal wall but not the thighs.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.front: Grade the degrees of perineal tear.
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.back: 1st — skin/vaginal mucosa only; 2nd — perineal muscles/body; 3rd — anal sphincter complex; 4th — through the anal mucosa. 3rd & 4th risk faecal incontinence.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.front: Why is an episiotomy usually made mediolaterally?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.back: To enlarge the vaginal outlet while directing the cut away from the perineal body & anal sphincter, reducing the risk of a 3rd/4th-degree tear.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.front: What is a Bartholin's cyst?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.back: Blockage of the duct of a greater vestibular gland → a painful (if infected) swelling at the posterolateral vaginal introitus.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.front: What is priapism?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.back: A persistent, painful erection (trapped blood in the corpora cavernosa) unrelated to arousal — a urological emergency.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.front: Recap: how does the pectinate line divide the anal canal?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.back: Above = visceral/insensate/portal drainage/internal iliac nodes (internal, painless haemorrhoids); below = somatic/very sensitive/systemic drainage/inguinal nodes (external, painful haemorrhoids & fissures).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.front: Where do anal fissures typically occur, and why are they painful?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.back: In the posterior midline, below the pectinate line — this is somatic (inferior rectal nerve) territory, so fissures are very painful.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.front: Which structures perforate the perineal membrane?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.back: The urethra (in both sexes) and the vagina (in the female).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.front: What lies within the pudendal (Alcock's) canal?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.back: The pudendal nerve and the internal pudendal vessels, running in the lateral wall of the ischioanal fossa (on obturator internus fascia).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.front: Which perineal glands lie in the deep pouch (male) versus the superficial pouch (female)?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.back: The bulbourethral (Cowper’s) glands lie in the deep pouch of the male; the greater vestibular (Bartholin’s) glands lie in the superficial pouch of the female.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.question: Each hip bone is formed by the fusion of which three bones?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.explanation: The ilium, ischium and pubis fuse at the acetabulum to form each hip bone (os coxae).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.question: Which structure forms the lateral border of the pelvic inlet (brim)?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.explanation: The lateral border of the pelvic inlet is the linea terminalis — the arcuate line of the ilium plus the pectineal line of the pubis.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.question: Which of the following forms the POSTERIOR border of the pelvic outlet?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.explanation: The pelvic outlet is bounded posteriorly by the tip of the coccyx (the sacral promontory is the posterior border of the inlet).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.question: The narrowest part of the birth canal is usually the distance between:
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.explanation: The interspinous (ischial spine to ischial spine) distance is normally the narrowest part of the pelvic canal.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.question: The diagonal conjugate is measured clinically because:
options: The true (obstetric) conjugate cannot be measured directly
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.explanation: The true/obstetric conjugate lies behind the symphysis and cannot be measured per vaginam, so the diagonal conjugate (promontory to inferior symphysis) is measured and ~1.5–2 cm is subtracted.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.question: Which feature is characteristic of the FEMALE pelvis?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.explanation: The female pelvis has a wide, U-shaped subpubic angle (>80°), a rounder inlet, a wider sciatic notch and everted spines — adaptations for childbirth.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.question: The sacrospinous ligament runs from the sacrum/coccyx to the:
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.explanation: The sacrospinous ligament attaches to the ischial spine; the sacrotuberous ligament attaches to the ischial tuberosity.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.question: The sacrospinous and sacrotuberous ligaments together:
options: Convert the sciatic notches into the greater and lesser sciatic foramina
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.explanation: The two ligaments span the sciatic notches, converting them into the greater and lesser sciatic foramina.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.question: Which structure is the key landmark dividing the greater sciatic foramen?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.explanation: Piriformis passes through the greater sciatic foramen; structures are described as passing above or below it.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.question: Which nerve/vessel exits ABOVE piriformis in the greater sciatic foramen?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.explanation: Only the superior gluteal nerve and vessels pass above piriformis; everything else (sciatic, inferior gluteal, pudendal, etc.) passes below.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.question: The pudendal nerve re-enters the perineum by passing through which structure?
options: The lesser sciatic foramen (around the ischial spine)
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.explanation: The pudendal nerve leaves via the greater sciatic foramen, hooks around the ischial spine/sacrospinous ligament, and re-enters the perineum through the lesser sciatic foramen.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.question: The obturator canal transmits which structures to the thigh?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.explanation: The obturator canal (at the superolateral obturator foramen) transmits the obturator nerve and vessels to the medial thigh.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.question: The pelvic diaphragm is composed of which muscles?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.explanation: The pelvic floor (pelvic diaphragm) is formed by levator ani (puborectalis, pubococcygeus, iliococcygeus) and coccygeus.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.question: Which part of levator ani forms a sling that maintains the anorectal angle?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.explanation: Puborectalis slings around the anorectal junction, maintaining the ~80–90° anorectal angle essential for faecal continence.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.question: The pelvic floor muscles are innervated principally by which spinal levels?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.explanation: Levator ani and the perineal muscles are supplied by S2–S4 (nerve to levator ani and the pudendal nerve).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.question: The pubic symphysis is classified as which type of joint?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.explanation: The pubic symphysis is a secondary cartilaginous joint (symphysis) with a fibrocartilage disc between hyaline-lined pubic bodies.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.question: Which hormone loosens the pelvic joints during pregnancy?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.explanation: Relaxin loosens the pubic symphysis and sacroiliac joints in pregnancy to increase pelvic diameters for delivery.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.question: A muscle forming the lateral wall of the pelvis is:
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.explanation: Obturator internus, covered by obturator fascia, forms the lateral wall of the pelvis; piriformis forms the posterior wall.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.question: The perineal body is clinically important because it is:
options: The origin of the sciatic nerve
The central tendon torn in a perineal tear / cut in an episiotomy
A branch of the internal iliac artery
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.explanation: The perineal body is the fibromuscular central tendon where the pelvic floor and perineal muscles meet — the key structure damaged in obstetric perineal tears and episiotomy.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.question: The sacroiliac joint is best described as:
options: Part synovial and part syndesmosis, very stable
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.explanation: The SI joint is a compound joint — synovial anteriorly and a syndesmosis (interosseous ligament) posteriorly — designed for stability and weight transfer with minimal movement.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.question: Weakness or injury of the pelvic floor most characteristically causes:
options: Pelvic organ prolapse and stress incontinence
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.explanation: Pelvic floor damage (childbirth, pudendal injury) leads to pelvic organ prolapse and stress urinary incontinence.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.question: Which of the following passes through the LESSER sciatic foramen?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.explanation: The lesser sciatic foramen transmits the obturator internus tendon, the nerve to obturator internus, and the pudendal neurovascular bundle re-entering the perineum.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.question: The trigone of the bladder is bounded by which structures?
options: The two ureteric orifices and the apex
The two ureteric orifices and the internal urethral orifice
The internal and external urethral orifices
The median and medial umbilical ligaments
The ureteric orifices and the ejaculatory ducts
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.explanation: The trigone is the smooth triangular area between the two ureteric orifices and the internal urethral orifice.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.question: Parasympathetic (S2–S4) stimulation of the bladder produces:
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.explanation: Parasympathetic pelvic splanchnic (S2–4) activity contracts the detrusor and relaxes the sphincter → voiding. Sympathetic activity stores urine.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.question: Sympathetic innervation of the bladder promotes continence by:
options: Relaxing the detrusor and contracting the internal sphincter
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.explanation: Sympathetic (L1–2, hypogastric) fibres relax the detrusor and contract the internal urethral sphincter — storage/continence.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.question: The ureter enters the pelvis by crossing over the:
options: Bifurcation of the common iliac artery
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.explanation: The ureter crosses the pelvic brim at the bifurcation of the common iliac artery, then descends on the lateral pelvic wall.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.question: Which is the NARROWEST point of the ureter, where stones most often impact?
options: Where it crosses the pelvic brim
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.explanation: The vesicoureteric junction (VUJ) is the narrowest of the three constrictions (PUJ, pelvic brim, VUJ).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.question: During a hysterectomy the ureter is at risk because:
options: It runs anterior to the uterine artery
The uterine artery crosses anterior/superior to it ('water under the bridge')
It lies within the broad ligament mesovarium
It passes through the inguinal canal
It is fused to the cervix
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.explanation: The uterine artery crosses superior (anterior) to the ureter near the cervix — 'water (ureter) under the bridge (artery)' — so the ureter can be clamped/ligated during hysterectomy.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.question: The oblique passage of the ureter through the bladder wall functions to:
options: Act as a valve preventing vesicoureteric reflux
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.explanation: The oblique intramural course is compressed as the bladder fills, forming a flap valve that prevents reflux of urine up the ureter.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.question: Which part of the male urethra is the shortest and least distensible?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.explanation: The membranous urethra passes through the external urethral sphincter; it is the shortest and least distensible, and a common site of injury.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.question: Fertilisation and the commonest site of ectopic pregnancy are both in the:
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.explanation: Fertilisation normally occurs in the ampulla of the uterine tube, which is also the commonest site of a tubal ectopic pregnancy.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.question: The three layers of the uterine wall from inside out are:
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.explanation: From inner to outer: endometrium (mucosa), myometrium (smooth muscle) and perimetrium (peritoneum).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.question: The normal uterus is described as:
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.explanation: The typical uterus is anteverted (cervix tips forward on the vagina) and anteflexed (body flexed forward on the cervix).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.question: The suspensory ligament of the ovary transmits the:
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.explanation: The suspensory ligament of the ovary (infundibulopelvic ligament) carries the ovarian artery, vein, nerves and lymphatics to the ovary.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.question: The uterine artery is a branch of the:
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.explanation: The uterine artery arises from the anterior division of the internal iliac artery; the ovarian artery (from the aorta) anastomoses with it.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.question: The lowest point of the peritoneal cavity in the female, where fluid collects, is the:
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.explanation: The rectouterine pouch (of Douglas), between the uterus and rectum, is the lowest point of the female peritoneal cavity and can be sampled via the posterior fornix.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.question: The round ligament of the uterus ends in the:
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.explanation: The round ligament (a gubernaculum remnant) runs from the uterine horn through the deep inguinal ring and inguinal canal to the labium majus.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.question: Most prostate carcinomas arise in which zone?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.explanation: Most prostate cancers arise in the peripheral (posterior) zone, which is why they are palpable on digital rectal examination; BPH affects the transitional zone.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.question: Benign prostatic hyperplasia characteristically involves which zone, causing what?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.explanation: BPH affects the transitional/periurethral zone, compressing the prostatic urethra and causing bladder outflow obstruction (hesitancy, poor stream, nocturia).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.question: The ejaculatory duct is formed by the union of the ductus deferens with the duct of the:
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.explanation: The ductus (vas) deferens joins the seminal vesicle duct to form the ejaculatory duct, which opens into the prostatic urethra.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.question: The pectinate line is clinically important because ABOVE it the anal canal is:
options: Autonomically innervated and insensate, draining to the portal system
Supplied by the inferior rectal artery
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.explanation: Above the pectinate line: visceral (autonomic) innervation (insensate), portal venous drainage and columnar epithelium — hence painless internal haemorrhoids.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.question: The superior rectal artery, supplying the upper rectum, is a branch of the:
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.explanation: The superior rectal artery is the continuation of the inferior mesenteric artery; the middle rectal arises from the internal iliac and the inferior rectal from the internal pudendal.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.question: A short, straight urethra explains why women are more prone to:
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.explanation: The female urethra is only ~4 cm and straight, allowing bacteria to ascend easily and predisposing to UTIs.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.question: The median umbilical ligament represents the remnant of the:
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.explanation: The median umbilical ligament is the fibrous remnant of the urachus, connecting the bladder apex to the umbilicus.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.question: The sacral plexus is formed by the anterior rami of which levels?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.explanation: The sacral plexus arises from the anterior rami of L4–S4, with the lumbosacral trunk (L4–L5) descending from the lumbar plexus.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.question: On which muscle does the sacral plexus lie?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.explanation: The sacral plexus lies on the anterior surface of piriformis on the posterior pelvic wall.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.question: The pudendal nerve arises from which roots?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.explanation: The pudendal nerve arises from S2, S3 and S4 — the same roots as the pelvic splanchnic nerves.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.question: Which sequence correctly describes the course of the pudendal nerve?
options: Lesser sciatic foramen → ischial tuberosity → greater sciatic foramen
Greater sciatic foramen → around the ischial spine → lesser sciatic foramen → Alcock's canal
Obturator canal → ischioanal fossa → greater sciatic foramen
Greater sciatic foramen → obturator canal → perineum
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.explanation: The pudendal nerve leaves via the greater sciatic foramen, hooks around the ischial spine, re-enters through the lesser sciatic foramen, and runs in the pudendal (Alcock's) canal.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.question: A pudendal nerve block is performed at which palpable landmark?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.explanation: The nerve is blocked where it hooks around the ischial spine, which is palpated transvaginally.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.question: Which branch of the pudendal nerve supplies the external anal sphincter?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.explanation: The inferior rectal (inferior anal) nerve supplies the external anal sphincter and perianal skin.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.question: The pelvic splanchnic nerves are which type of fibre, and from which roots?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.explanation: The pelvic splanchnic nerves (nervi erigentes) are parasympathetic and arise from S2–S4 — the sacral parasympathetic outflow.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.question: Parasympathetic stimulation of the pelvic viscera produces all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Relaxation of the internal anal sphincter
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.explanation: Ejaculation is a SYMPATHETIC function ('shoot'); the parasympathetics produce voiding, erection and increased bowel motility.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.question: According to 'point and shoot', erection is mediated by:
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.explanation: Parasympathetic (S2–4) fibres 'Point' (erection); sympathetic fibres 'Shoot' (emission/ejaculation).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.question: Damage to the sympathetic pelvic supply characteristically causes:
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.explanation: Sympathetic fibres close the internal urethral sphincter during ejaculation; their loss allows semen to pass backward into the bladder (retrograde ejaculation).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.question: The superior hypogastric plexus lies:
options: On either side of the rectum
Anterior to the sacral promontory / lower aorta
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.explanation: The superior hypogastric plexus is a midline, mainly sympathetic plexus anterior to the sacral promontory and lower aorta; it divides into the hypogastric nerves.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.question: The inferior hypogastric plexus is formed by the hypogastric nerve plus which nerves?
options: The pelvic splanchnic (and sacral splanchnic) nerves
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.explanation: The inferior hypogastric plexus is formed by the hypogastric nerve (sympathetic) plus the pelvic splanchnic nerves (parasympathetic) and sacral splanchnics; it lies beside the rectum.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.question: Which autonomic division promotes urine STORAGE?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.explanation: Sympathetic (L1–2) activity relaxes the detrusor and contracts the internal urethral sphincter → storage; parasympathetics cause voiding.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.question: Nerve-sparing prostatectomy aims to preserve which fibres, and why?
options: The cavernous (parasympathetic) nerves from the inferior hypogastric plexus; for erectile function
The sciatic nerve; for leg power
The obturator nerve; for thigh sensation
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.explanation: The cavernous nerves carry parasympathetic (erectile) fibres from the inferior hypogastric plexus; preserving them protects erectile function.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.question: Visceral pain from a structure ABOVE the pelvic pain line is carried by ____ afferents and referred to ____.
options: Sympathetic; the suprapubic region and lower back (T12–L2)
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.explanation: Structures touching the peritoneum (above the pain line) send pain via sympathetic afferents to T12–L2 → referred to the suprapubic area and lower back.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.question: Visceral pain from a structure BELOW the pelvic pain line (e.g. the cervix) is referred to:
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.explanation: Subperitoneal structures (below the pain line) send pain via parasympathetic (pelvic splanchnic) afferents to S2–4 → referred to the perineum.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.question: In the second stage of labour, perineal pain is transmitted mainly by the:
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.explanation: First-stage (uterine/cervical) pain travels via T10–L1; second-stage perineal pain travels via the pudendal nerve (S2–4), the basis of a pudendal block.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.question: Cauda equina syndrome from S2–S4 compression classically causes:
options: Saddle anaesthesia, painless retention and bowel/sexual dysfunction
Loss of the ankle jerk only
Groin pain with a normal neurological exam
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.explanation: S2–4 root compression produces saddle anaesthesia, painless urinary retention and bowel/sexual dysfunction — a surgical emergency.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.question: The largest nerve of the sacral plexus, with roots L4–S3, is the:
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.explanation: The sciatic nerve (L4–S3) is the largest nerve in the body, supplying the hamstrings and, via its divisions, the whole leg and foot.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.question: The coccygeal plexus is formed from which roots?
options: S4, S5 and the coccygeal nerve
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.explanation: The coccygeal plexus arises from S4, S5 and the coccygeal nerve and gives the anococcygeal nerves.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.question: Which statement about the pelvic parasympathetic outflow is correct?
options: It travels with the pudendal nerve
It is the only parasympathetic outflow arising from the sacral cord (S2–4)
It arises from the lateral horn of T1–L2
It synapses in the superior cervical ganglion
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Aut.explanation: The pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2–4) are the only parasympathetic outflow that arises from the sacral spinal cord rather than a cranial nerve.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.question: The main arterial supply to the pelvis is the:
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.explanation: The internal iliac artery, arising from the common iliac at the pelvic brim, is the principal blood supply of the pelvis.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.question: Which three arteries form the POSTERIOR division of the internal iliac artery?
options: Superior vesical, middle rectal, inferior gluteal
Superior gluteal, inferior gluteal, internal pudendal
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.explanation: The posterior division gives the iliolumbar, lateral sacral and superior gluteal arteries ('I Love Sex').

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.question: Which artery exits the pelvis ABOVE piriformis?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.explanation: The superior gluteal artery leaves via the greater sciatic foramen above piriformis; the inferior gluteal and internal pudendal pass below it.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.question: The 'corona mortis' refers to an aberrant:
options: Obturator artery arising from the inferior epigastric artery
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.explanation: An aberrant/accessory obturator artery from the inferior epigastric crosses the superior pubic ramus and can bleed torrentially in hernia repair or pelvic fracture — the 'crown of death'.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.question: The gonadal (ovarian/testicular) arteries arise from the:
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.explanation: The gonadal arteries arise directly from the abdominal aorta at ~L2, reflecting the gonads' high embryological origin.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.question: The superior rectal artery is the continuation of the:
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.explanation: The superior rectal artery is the direct continuation of the inferior mesenteric artery, supplying the upper rectum.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.question: Which artery is the principal supply of the perineum and erectile tissue?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.explanation: The internal pudendal artery supplies the perineum; its deep arteries of the penis/clitoris fill the erectile tissue.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.question: The left gonadal (ovarian/testicular) vein drains into the:
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.explanation: The left gonadal vein drains into the left renal vein; the right gonadal vein drains directly into the IVC.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.question: Batson's vertebral venous plexus is clinically important because it:
options: Provides a valveless route for prostate cancer to spread to the spine
Is the main supply of the cord
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.explanation: The valveless internal vertebral venous plexus communicates with the pelvic plexuses, allowing prostate/pelvic cancer to metastasise to the vertebrae, pelvis and brain.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.question: The superior rectal vein drains into the ____ system, creating a portosystemic anastomosis.
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.explanation: The superior rectal vein drains to the portal system (via the IMV); it anastomoses with the systemic middle/inferior rectal veins — the site of rectal varices.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.question: Testicular cancer spreads first to which lymph nodes?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.explanation: The testis drains to the para-aortic nodes along the gonadal vessels (its embryological origin); scrotal SKIN, by contrast, drains to the superficial inguinal nodes.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.question: The lower anal canal (below the pectinate line) drains lymph to the:
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.explanation: Below the pectinate line the anal canal (somatic territory) drains to the superficial inguinal nodes; above it drains to the internal iliac nodes.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.question: Most pelvic viscera drain lymph ultimately to which nodes before the lumbar trunks?
options: Internal iliac → common iliac → para-aortic (lumbar) nodes
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.explanation: Pelvic viscera drain to internal iliac → common iliac → lateral aortic/para-aortic (lumbar) nodes, then to the lumbar trunks and cisterna chyli.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.question: The ovary drains lymph to the para-aortic nodes because:
options: It shares drainage with the bladder
Its lymphatics follow the ovarian vessels back to their embryological origin
It lies below the pelvic pain line
It drains via the round ligament only
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.explanation: Ovarian (and testicular) lymphatics follow the gonadal vessels to the para-aortic nodes, reflecting the gonad's abdominal embryological origin.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.question: The internal iliac artery can be ligated for pelvic haemorrhage because:
options: The pelvis has no other supply
It only supplies the gluteal region
The external iliac takes over the bladder
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.explanation: Collateral pathways (rectal, uterine-ovarian, cruciate/trochanteric) keep the pelvis perfused, so ligation controls bleeding without ischaemia.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.question: The obturator artery leaves the pelvis through the:
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.explanation: The obturator artery passes with the obturator nerve through the obturator canal to the medial thigh.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.question: Which part of the uterus drains lymph to the para-aortic nodes (and partly via the round ligament to inguinal nodes)?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.explanation: The uterine fundus and tubal angle drain to the para-aortic nodes (and along the round ligament to the superficial inguinal); the body → external iliac; the cervix → internal/external iliac + sacral.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.question: Rectal varices arise from an anastomosis between the superior rectal vein and the:
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.explanation: The superior rectal vein (portal) anastomoses with the middle and inferior rectal veins (systemic); portal hypertension dilates these into rectal varices.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.question: A midline branch of the aorta contributing to the posterior pelvic wall is the:
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.explanation: The median sacral artery is a small unpaired branch of the aorta running over the sacrum in the midline.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.question: Prostate cancer characteristically produces which type of bony metastases, via Batson's plexus?
options: Sclerotic (osteoblastic) lesions of the lumbar spine and pelvis
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Ly.explanation: Prostate cancer spreads via the valveless vertebral venous (Batson's) plexus to the lumbar spine and pelvis, classically producing sclerotic/osteoblastic metastases.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.question: The boundaries of the perineum are the pubic symphysis, the coccyx and the:
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.explanation: The perineal diamond is bounded by the pubic symphysis (anterior), the ischial tuberosities (lateral) and the coccyx (posterior).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.question: A line between the ischial tuberosities divides the perineum into which two triangles?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.explanation: The interischial line divides the perineum into the anterior urogenital triangle and the posterior anal triangle.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.question: The superficial perineal pouch lies between the perineal membrane and:
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.explanation: The superficial pouch lies between the perineal membrane (above) and Colles' fascia (below).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.question: Which structure is found in the DEEP perineal pouch?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.explanation: The deep pouch contains the external urethral sphincter, deep transverse perinei and (in the male) the bulbourethral glands; the erectile tissue and superficial muscles are in the superficial pouch.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.question: Which muscle covers the crura (corpora cavernosa) and helps maintain erection?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.explanation: Ischiocavernosus covers the crura (corpora cavernosa) and compresses them to maintain erection; bulbospongiosus covers the bulb (corpus spongiosum).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.question: All the muscles of the perineum are innervated by the:
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.explanation: Every perineal muscle is supplied by the pudendal nerve (S2–S4) via its perineal and inferior rectal branches.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.question: The greater vestibular (Bartholin's) glands are located in the ____ and are homologous to the ____.
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.explanation: Bartholin's glands lie in the female superficial perineal pouch and are homologous to the male bulbourethral (Cowper's) glands.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.question: The corpus spongiosum is important because it:
options: Transmits the spongy urethra and expands as the glans
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.explanation: The single, ventral corpus spongiosum transmits the spongy urethra, forms the bulb proximally and expands distally as the glans penis.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.question: The ischioanal fossa is primarily filled with ____ and contains the ____ in its lateral wall.
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.explanation: The ischioanal fossa is a fat-filled space; its lateral wall contains the pudendal (Alcock's) canal carrying the pudendal nerve and internal pudendal vessels.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.question: An ischioanal abscess can spread to the opposite side to form a horseshoe abscess because the fossae:
options: Communicate posteriorly behind the anal canal
Drain to the same lymph nodes
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.explanation: The two ischioanal fossae communicate posteriorly (deep to the anococcygeal body), so infection can track across into a horseshoe abscess.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.question: The internal anal sphincter is:
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.explanation: The internal anal sphincter is a thickening of the circular smooth muscle, involuntary and tonically contracted; the external anal sphincter is voluntary (pudendal).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.question: The external anal sphincter is supplied by which nerve?
options: The inferior rectal branch of the pudendal nerve
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.explanation: The external anal sphincter (skeletal, voluntary) is supplied by the inferior rectal branch of the pudendal nerve.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.question: A ruptured bulbar (spongy) urethra spills urine into the superficial pouch, which then tracks to the scrotum and abdominal wall but NOT the thighs because:
options: Colles' fascia is attached to the fascia lata and perineal membrane
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.explanation: Colles' fascia is continuous with Scarpa's fascia (abdomen) but is attached laterally to the fascia lata and posteriorly to the perineal membrane, so urine spreads up the abdomen and into the scrotum but is blocked from the thighs.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.question: A third-degree perineal tear involves the:
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.explanation: A 3rd-degree tear extends into the anal sphincter complex; 1st = skin, 2nd = perineal muscles/body, 4th = through the anal mucosa.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.question: An episiotomy is typically performed mediolaterally in order to:
options: Avoid the perineal body and anal sphincter
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.explanation: A mediolateral episiotomy directs the incision away from the perineal body and anal sphincter, reducing the risk of a 3rd/4th-degree extension.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.question: The perineal membrane is perforated by the urethra and, in the female, also the:
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.explanation: The perineal membrane is perforated by the urethra in both sexes and by the vagina in the female.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.question: The female homologue of the penile corpus spongiosum / bulb of the penis is the:
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.explanation: The bulbs of the vestibule (flanking the vaginal opening) are the female homologue of the penile bulb/corpus spongiosum; the clitoris corresponds to the corpora cavernosa.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.question: Anal fissures characteristically occur in the posterior midline BELOW the pectinate line and are painful because this region is:
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.explanation: Below the pectinate line the anal canal has somatic sensory innervation (inferior rectal nerve), so fissures there are very painful; the posterior midline is relatively poorly perfused.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.question: Which glands lie in the deep perineal pouch of the male?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.explanation: The bulbourethral (Cowper's) glands lie in the male deep perineal pouch and drain into the spongy urethra.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.question: A persistent, painful erection unrelated to sexual arousal, from trapped blood in the corpora cavernosa, is called:
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Perineum.explanation: Priapism is a persistent painful erection due to trapped blood in the corpora cavernosa — a urological emergency.
